title: Incident review: KV cache shard skew + eviction heuristic regression — customer SLO impact
summary: A gradual regression in the KV cache eviction heuristic combined with an allocator rounding bug produced persistent shard skew across GPUs. The skew caused a subset of requests to experience repeated cold-KV-cache misses, increasing p99 and causing SLO misses for one large hosted customer. A targeted rollback of the heuristic and a coordinated shard rebalancer hotfix restored normal distribution and resolved SLO violations. This document captures timeline, root cause analysis, validation steps, and follow-ups.
content:
Summary:

On 2026-08-04 we received a customer escalation (Acme Retail, high-volume hosted) reporting p99 generation latency regressions beginning ~2026-08-03 22:00 UTC. The customer observed intermittent 2–4x p99 increases on their production traffic; average latency and throughput were largely unchanged. Redwood SLO dashboards showed p99 increases from ~210ms to ~620ms for the route backed by the medium Llama variant.

Impact:
- Customer: p99 SLO breached for 3 of 6 rolling 1-hour windows across 2026-08-03 22:00 – 2026-08-04 06:00 UTC.
- Internally: alerting triggered on p99 anomaly and on an increase in KV cache miss ratio for the affected model variant.
- Mitigation: routed customer to a compatible model variant fallback for 1 hour while investigation progressed.

Detection and initial triage:
- 2026-08-04 01:05 UTC: oncall SRE noticed a correlation between p99 bursts and increased KV cache miss rate on a subset of GPU nodes serving the customer.
- Quick inspection of metrics: per-node KV cache occupancy distributions showed heavy imbalance: some nodes had 3x the expected cache occupancy while many had <20% occupancy.
- Flamegraphs and per-request traces indicated that requests hitting under-populated nodes paid a higher per-token latency due to repeated K/V lookups falling back to model recomputation.

Hypothesis generation:
We focused on two things that changed in the last two weeks: (A) a change to the KV cache eviction heuristic (INF-4180) intended to prefer evicting long-tail keys, and (B) a small allocator rounding tweak that changed how shards are sized per-GPU when memory quantization margins are tight (PR #1179). Hypotheses: either the heuristic caused persistent hotspotting of certain shards, or the allocator rounding produced unequal shard counts leading to skew between GPUs.

Deep dive and data collection:
- Replayed sampling traces across affected nodes and compared cached key histograms across the fleet. Keys that should have been evenly distributed by consistent-hash showed clumping on 6 nodes.
- Git bisect and deploy history: heuristic deployed 2026-07-21; allocator rounding change deployed 2026-07-28. Customer telemetry showed first noticeable drift 2026-08-02.
- Microbenchmarks: locally reproducing the eviction heuristic on synthetic traces showed it reduced churn in steady-state, but under realistic allocation quotas + the allocator rounding change we observed a pathological steady-state where a small set of shards captured >60% of cache residency.
- Heap and kernel traces: no GPU OOMs, but slightly higher memory pressure on hotspot nodes (consistent with more resident KV entries).

Root cause analysis (conclusion):
Two interacting regressions produced the impact:
1) Allocator rounding bug (PR #1179) caused per-GPU shard counts to be rounded in a way that some GPUs received one fewer shard than intended when operating near quantization thresholds. This made the logical distribution of shards per GPU uneven in a predictable subset of placements.
2) The new eviction heuristic (INF-4180) favored evicting long-tail keys; when combined with uneven shard counts it caused a feedback loop where the smaller-shard GPUs would evict aggressively and lose hot keys, while larger-shard GPUs retained more of the hot set. Over time hot keys became concentrated on the larger-shard GPUs and requests that landed on small-shard GPUs experienced repeated cache misses.

Why p99 increased but mean stayed similar:
The majority of requests still hit larger-shard GPUs and saw normal latencies; however, a small fraction (roughly 4–6%) of requests consistently hit the under-populated nodes and incurred additional recomputation costs, inflating p99 without materially changing mean.

Mitigations and hotfix applied:
- Short term (2026-08-04 03:20 UTC): rolled back allocator rounding tweak to previous behavior on the affected pool; rolled back eviction heuristic to the pre-2026-07-21 parameters for the implicated model variant.
- Medium term (2026-08-04 10:00 UTC): rolled out a shard rebalancer that performs conservative reshuffling to equalize shard counts across GPUs when placement changes leave residual imbalance.
- Additional immediate workaround: added a temporary routing policy that biases requests away from nodes with occupancy <30% until rebalancer completed.

Hotfix validation (what we ran to be confident):
1) Synthetic load replay: used customer-like traffic trace (anonymized) to replay 24 hours of traffic in a staging-shadow cluster with both the original and the patched runtime. Observed p99 return to baseline within 2 hours for patched run.
2) Microbenchmarks: repeated eviction microbenchmark across many shard-count permutations to ensure no further pathological clustering; verified approximately uniform key occupancy within ±8% after rebalancer.
3) Canary rollout: incrementally bumped production traffic to patched nodes and monitored p50/p95/p99, per-node cache occupancy, and cache miss ratio for 30-minute intervals. No SLOs were breached post-rollout.
4) Customer verification: coordinated with Acme Retail to run an internal verification window; they reported no p99 anomalies for a 4-hour verification period and closed the escalation.

Post-deployment monitoring and artifacts:
- Dashboards added: per-deployment shard-count distribution, per-node cache-residency histogram, and a derived metric: fraction of request-ids that experienced >1 KV miss per request.
- Alerting adjusted: p99 anomaly alert now triggers a secondary alarm if the per-node occupancy 90th/10th percentile ratio exceeds 2.0.

Lessons learned:
- Small allocator tweaks can have outsized systemic impact when combined with cache heuristics; integration testing that exercises both placement and eviction behavior under realistic per-GPU quantization margins was insufficient.
- Observability gap: we lacked a rolling, fleet-wide shard-count histogram metric that would have flagged the skew earlier.
- Deploy sequencing: multiple independent changes to placement/eviction logic deployed within 7 days increased combinatorial risk; we need a tighter policy for dependent runtime changes.

Action items (owners and ETA):
- INF-4321: Add integration test that replays realistic placement + eviction interactions with quantized allocations (owner: Xiaoyu Chen, ETA: 2026-09-02).
- INF-4322: Implement continuous shard-distribution telemetry (owner: Liam O'Connor, ETA: 2026-08-20).
- INF-4323: Extend canary gating to include a shard-uniformity check for all runtime placement/ejection PRs (owner: Diego Ramirez, ETA: 2026-08-25).
- INF-4324: Postmortem doc and internal blameless review (owner: Maya Patel, ETA: 2026-08-18).

Appendix — Validation artifacts and quick summary of numbers:
- Pre-incident baseline p99 (affected route): ~210ms. Incident p99 peak: ~620ms. Post-hotfix p99: ~230ms within 2 hours.
- Fraction of requests hitting under-populated nodes during incident windows: 4–6%.
- Worst-case per-request extra compute time when cache missed repeatedly: measured as +150–420ms depending on sequence length.
- Rebalancer effect: reduced worst 90/10 occupancy ratio from 3.9 -> 1.2 in staging replay.

Notes and references:
- Linked runtime PR that introduced allocator rounding: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1179
- Jira: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/INF-4321 (investigation), INF-4322 (telemetry), INF-4323 (canary gate), INF-4324 (review)
